title: France v Springboks: Five takeaways as 'peerless' Antoine Dupont answers 'truly great' question to down South Africa - Planet Rugby
content: Antoine Dupont celebrates with fans after France beat South Africa. France beat South Africa 21-19 at the Stade de France on Friday night, an injury-ravaged side winning the air whilst the Springboks won the scrum, and Antoine Dupont produced the finest individual display of his career to hold it all together. What a night. Honestly, by the hour mark you’d stopped trying to count the cards, the reviews and the bodies on the floor, and simply stood in Saint-Denis and watched two of the best sides in the world go at each other with a ferocity that belonged in a World Cup knockout, which, three years on from that quarter-final, is more or less what this felt like, with 20,000 South Africans having turned the streets around the stadium green and gold by mid-afternoon. The context has to come in one breath, because it matters. France were without Matthieu Jalibert, Romain Ntamack, Antoine Hastoy, Thomas Ramos, Emmanuel Meafou, Thibaud Flament, Demba Bamba and Lenni Nouchi, lost Julien Marchand to a thigh strain shortly before kick-off, had lost nine of their last ten Tests against South Africa and the last five at this ground, and then collected three yellow cards along the way. They still won. Quite how, might remain a question South Africa will ask for an age, but the answer lay with the truly great Dupont. Make no mistake, this was rugby at the top of Everest, and it came down to two different games being played on the same pitch. France won the air and the broken field, kicking to grass and scoring three tries in 17 first-half minutes; South Africa won the set-piece, scored all three of their tries off the lineout and maul, and turned 21-7 at the break into 21-19 with a scrum 40 metres out in the 78th minute. In between stood two defences that were breathtaking, ferocious, unyielding, indefatigable. And holding the whole thing together, wearing ten and playing mostly at nine, was that man Toto. South Africa threw everything at them, and this was no fluke. It was a match won by heart over head, and the Stade de France gave France an extra man even when they had 14. It was fitting it was Dupont who delivered the knock-out blow, winning a ruck to close South Africa out at the final whistle. Just wow. Here’s the thing about France’s kicking plan: it was built to keep the ball on the field and remove the driving maul from the game. Fabien Galthié brought Maxime Petitjean in from Toulon to work on it, and from the first ten minutes the intent was obvious, France kicking to grass rather than touch and daring the Springboks to run it back at them. Every kick that stays in play is a lineout the Boks don’t get, and a lineout they don’t get is a maul they can’t set and a corner they can’t go to, which against this pack is half their attacking game gone before it starts. Springboks player ratings: ‘Daft’ Jasper Wiese costs Rassie’s men as Bomb Squad lacks knock-out punch It produced the tries, too. Théo Attissogbe’s 50:22 drew a late shot on the kicker, the penalty came back to where the kick came down, and from the next attack Yoram Moefana’s pass went off Kalvin Gourgues’ head and forward to Attissogbe, who scored; the TMO had a long look, but a knock-on needs a hand or an arm, and the try stood. Eight minutes later Dupont slid a grubber into the space behind the defence and Louis Bielle-Biarrey, the electric scooter himself, did the rest. For all that, France should have been out of sight long before the Bok bench arrived. They could have been 14 up inside the first quarter of an hour, Bielle-Biarrey bundled into touch and Aaron Grandidier-Nkanang a metre short, and when they kicked a penalty to the corner, Lood de Jager stole the throw from Peato Mauvaka, who’d only come into the side when Marchand, picked partly for his jackal, was ruled out. Add three penalties that missed touch and a kick at goal that missed at 67 minutes, and France left enough out there to have won this at a canter. The hole in the plan was the penalty count, and the cards that almost cost them the game, mostly as their props held on like men hanging out of a broken rollercoaster. France conceded 14 on the night, every one of them handing back the lineout the kicking was designed to take away, and South Africa finished with 15 lineouts at 100 per cent. Jan-Hendrik Wessels’ maul try at 29 minutes came straight after back-to-back French penalties in their own 22, and Malcolm Marx’s at 71 came off the same platform. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. Rassie Erasmus swapped his entire front-row an hour before kick-off, as he did in Cape Town in August, starting Wessels, Gerhard Steenekamp and Thomas du Toit on a dry, still night and keeping Ox Nche, Marx and Wilco Louw for later; at 21-7 down he couldn’t wait for later, and sent all three on at 37 minutes. France conceded nince scrum penalties, six of them after the switch, with Nche taking Régis Montagne apart on the tighthead side until Montagne went to the bin at 68 minutes and Cameron Woki had to come off so Sipili Falatea could return. That’s a back-rower lost just to keep the scrum contested, with the Boks camped in French territory. How thin the margin was shows in the numbers, with South Africa having 55 per cent of the ball, 58 per cent of the territory, 150 carries to France’s 112 and 188 post-contact metres to 102. The team sheet said Dupont at ten and Maxime Lucu at nine. Within a minute Dupont was at the base, and for the rest of the night la charnière swapped everything, nine and ten changing from phase to phase in a hybrid hinge that took Erasmus’s favourite selection word and turned it back on him. Galthié called them “two icons in France” in the week, and the first try showed why the pairing works: Dupont passed out, Lucu looped round him as the extra man, very rugby league, and Aaron Grandidier-Nkanang finished in the corner. Lucu was fabulous until his yellow, his tempo and the length of his kicking giving France a second playmaker who could take the ball off Dupont’s shoulder at speed, and when he went to the bin for a high shot on Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, Gourgues, whom the Boks had been expected to target at 13 and who was phenomenal instead, stepped in at fly-half for ten minutes as a third man in the hinge. France player ratings v Springboks: ‘Perfect’ Antoine Dupont drops masterclass in famous Les Bleus win But this was Dupont’s night, and I’ll say it plainly: it’s one of the greatest individual performance I’ve ever seen in the 452 Test matches I have covered. He controlled the Test in every facet there is, kicking, rucking, tackling, carrying and distributing; he made two line breaks, put the grubber in for Bielle-Biarrey, tracked 30 metres back across the field to take out Kurt-Lee Arendse with the line at his mercy, held Pieter-Steph du Toit up over the line almost on his own, forced Damian Willemse into spilling a high ball at 75 minutes, and then, with the Boks running from that last scrum, won the turnover that ended it. South African supporters have been on his back for years. This was his answer, delivered at the ground where France had lost their last five Tests against them. He was peerless. Both defences were sensational, and the numbers explain why the scoreboard stayed so tight for so long. The Boks made 75 tackles in the first 23 minutes and still conceded 14 points, which tells you how much France asked of them early; by the end it was France making the tackles, 173 to 141, with François Cros top of the sheet on 17, two of them dominant, and Moefana on 15. Cros was everywhere he needed to be, a scything machine. His turnover early in the second half sent France the length of the field, and his tackle in the 77th minute, with the Boks coming down the middle, was the hit of the night, one that underlined everything that defines desperation and everything that makes Cros the formidable force he is; Esteban Capilla won a turnover on France’s own line, and when Montagne’s yellow left France short again, they held out against a Bok scrum 40 metres out and everything South Africa threw at them from it. France v South Africa, LIVE BLOG: Coverage of the Nations Championship fixture On the other side, Damian de Allende made 15 tackles, Jesse Kriel was outstanding in midfield, Pieter-Steph du Toit carried 18 times, and Cobus Reinach and Cameron Hanekom changed the tempo off the bench, Reinach scoring the try at 50 minutes that brought it back to 21-14. Feinberg-Mngomezulu fell away badly, though, and the moment that defined his night came at 38 minutes, when he broke through with two men on his inside shoulder and the posts at his mercy and didn’t pass. There was plenty for Andrea Piardi to manage. Lood de Jager’s yellow at 17 minutes cost the Boks 14 points; Jasper Wiese’s arm into Gourgues’ head at a clear-out was upgraded to red by the bunker; and when Grandidier-Nkanang knocked on deliberately with South Africa two on none and no French cover behind him, Piardi sent him to the bin without awarding the penalty try. The law asks whether a try would probably have been scored, and readers can judge that one for themselves, and we know where we sit. South Africa might be rightly furious about that. Find a front-row. France have the most dangerous attack in the world and, on this evidence, a scrum that can’t survive the last half-hour against the Springboks, which a year out from the World Cup is the one problem Galthié can’t design his way around, however much he enjoyed designing a solution at half-back this week. Argentina come to the Stade de France on Saturday, November 21, the same day the Springboks go to Dublin, with the Nations Championship finals in London the following weekend, and the French scrum will be the first thing the Pumas look at. It wasn’t a World Cup, and nothing will make up for the disappointment of 2023, but given France’s injury list this was a game of the very highest calibre, and one of their greatest ever nights. It will never make up for the 2023 loss, but the Stade de France rocks on Friday the 13th. Breathtaking. title: Honda's popular CR-V SUV going '100% hybrid' in sign of larger trends - USA Today
content: Why are competitors like Toyota and Hyundai expanding hybrid offerings? Honda is converting its most popular U.S car, the CR-V, into a "100% hybrid" vehicle -meaning no solely gas-powered versions will be made - as car shoppers continue flocking to fuel efficient vehicles with gas prices remaining high near $4 per gallon. The Japanese company said in a Nov. 12 news release "the 2028 Honda CR-V will arrive next year, powered exclusively by an all-new two-motor Honda Hybrid system." "With a 100% hybrid powertrain, the next-generation Honda CR-V will further expand the appeal of America's most popular SUV as demand for hybrid-electric vehicles reaches record levels," Luis Guerra, assistant vice president of Honda National Auto Sales, said in a statement. The announcement comes as several of Honda's competitors have gone all in on hybrids and their customers appear to be receiving them well. Cars.com said hybrids now make up 12.2% of new vehicles for sale, up from 11.4% a year ago and 8% two years ago. Additionally, in the first half of 2026, 22% of shoppers said they would consider a hybrid vehicle, which was up from 20% in 2025, according to Kelley Blue Book. "While durability and safety remain the most influential purchase considerations across all shoppers, affordability and fuel economy have become increasingly important over the past five years," Kelley Blue Book said. The USA TODAY Cars team took a look at why Honda is making the CR-V hybrid now, why it is the company's most important vehicle, and why Honda's competitors are also flooding showrooms with hybrids now. Honda said it decided now was the right time to make a hybrid of its most popular car because it was listening to its customers. "Increasing sales of hybrid-electric vehicles is key to Honda's overall growth strategy," the company said. "With hybrid and SUV consideration at all-time highs, the 7th-generation CR-V is the first of several hybrid models Honda plans to launch in North America by 2030." Honda currently offers the CR-V in both gas-powered and hybrid formats. The 2027 hybrid CR-V start at $36,030 and it will be available in seven trims. The company said it has a two-motor hybrid system, and it will have 204 horsepower. The hybrid version of the current CR-V gets an EPA-estimated 43 mpg in city driving and 36 mpg on highways. The CR-V has been Honda's top-selling U.S. car since 2017, when it first surpassed the Civic sedan for that title. Here's how the CR-V has sold in the U.S. since then: Carmakers are selling more hybrids than ever because, as several of them cut back on their EV production at the start of President Trump's administration, the hybrids they were already making became more attractive to consumers as the salience of fuel efficiency increased for car shoppers. In 2025, there were 13,929,600 non-plug-in hybrid vehicles and 1,765,700 plug-in hybrid vehicles registered on U.S. roads, according to the U.S. Department of Energy's Alternative Fuel Data Center. By comparison, the agency said there were 5,689,100 fully electric cars and over 240 million gas cars registered in the nation last year. At the start of the second Trump administration, the White House and Republicans in Congress moved to eliminate the popular $7,500 EV tax credit offered by the federal government since the tail end of former President George W. Bush's administration. Trump also moved to cut funding for electric vehicle chargers approved by former President Joe Biden. Carmakers reacted to the shifting headwinds in Washington by cutting back on many of their plans to introduce new electric models. But automakers that have been marketing hybrids for years, like Honda, Toyota, Hyundai and Kia, have reaped the benefits as gas prices surged. High gas prices for most of this year have driven shoppers to consider hybrids a lot more. The average price of gas on Friday, Nov. 13 was $3.87, according to AAA. That's up from an average of $3.07 on Nov. 13, 2025. Despite those increases, polls show there is still hesitancy among some drivers about going fully electric. Car buyers have been telling pollsters for years that they have major concerns about the battery range of electric cars. The concern has bubbled up so often that it has been dubbed "range anxiety." According to a poll released in January 2026 by the EVs for All America group, an advocacy group that works with car manufacturers to push U.S. and state lawmakers to adopt EV-friendly policies, 20% of 600 respondents to a poll intended to survey potential EV buyers in 2025 said their top concern about plug-in models is the charger networks being unreliable. That's where hybrids come in. Most regular hybrids have batteries that get their power from regenerative braking, according to Edmunds, which is an automotive industry research group that also tests and reviews cars. That means drivers don't have to worry about hooking up to a charger at all. Hybrid cars operate on battery usually for shorter, low-speed portions of the trip and switch to gas when necessary for longer, higher-speed trips. Some hybrid cars can get over 500 miles on a single tank. Plug-in hybrid electric vehicles, or PHEVs as they are sometimes referred to, usually have a significantly larger battery pack that allows the car to be operated on electric power for stretches of time that can last about 40 to 50 miles, according to Edmunds. Plug-in hybrids have been seen as a compromise option for people who want to experience electric driving but are not ready to commit to driving a fully electric car. title: NetChoice v. James (New York Censorship Labels) - NetChoice
content:
Case Status: Complaint filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York
Latest Update: November 13, 2026
Attorneys: Websites cannot be forced to act as mouthpieces for New York’s views about social media. NetChoice’s newest lawsuit challenges New York’s latest attempt to control and compel online speech. SB S4505 forces websites to display New York’s preferred message about social media use–messages that cannot be skipped by users and get larger and more frequent over time. And just like laws in Colorado, Minnesota, and California that NetChoice is already challenging, SB S4505 is flatly unconstitutional. The goal is to deter users from online services and push the government’s controversial views on social media. This is compelled speech, a direct violation of the First Amendment. New York’s SB S4505 singles out the websites where free speech thrives today, especially on political and cultural issues. The First Amendment bars the government from making private actors speak for it, whether the medium be a billboard, a newspaper, or a website. States cannot do by “warning label” what they’re forbidden from doing by outright ban, and trying to chill speech through stigma is still censorship. A federal court already blocked Colorado’s nearly identical law in NetChoice v. Weiser, and New York’s is even more extreme. The state is using legitimate concerns about mental health as cover for a law that’s really about power. The science on how online services affect mental health and well-being is still emerging and contradictory, and it’s even thinner for adults. There’s no credible evidence that a government warning label improves youth well-being. Users will ultimately pay the price. The state’s goal is to annoy or scare people away from websites whose content it dislikes, cluttering their screens with government messages they must sit through no matter how many times they’ve seen them. Lawmakers who want a better online environment for kids should pursue constitutional measures like those in NetChoice’s Digital Safety Shield for America. New York is free to share its own views through public campaigns and resources, but it can’t force private websites to speak for it. NetChoice’s complaint filed on November 13, 2026, in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York.

Last month, we wrote that Congress had passed the “Bankruptcy Threshold Adjustment Act,” which would raise the debt limit for eligibility for subchapter V as soon as the president signed it into law. That happened on November 10, 2026. Thus, effective as of that date, debtors with noncontingent, liquidated debt[1] that is not more than $7,500,000 now may be eligible for relief under this part of the Bankruptcy Code. For cases filed on or before November 9, 2026, the subchapter V debt limit remains $3,424,000. There is no sunset for this adjustment. The amount will be adjusted for inflation every three years along with most other bankruptcy statutory limits and amounts. The chapter 13 debt limit is also adjusted by this new law. As of November 10, 2026, there is a single $2,750,000 debt limit for both secured and unsecured debt. This debt limit will also be adjusted for inflation going forward. Miller Canfield regularly assists clients in navigating the Bankruptcy Code and protecting their rights under it. Should you have any questions or need any assistance, please feel free to contact us. [1] Generally speaking, a “contingent” debt is one that requires some event to happen before it is owed (e.g., a warranty claim owed only if a covered part fails). “Noncontingent” debts are those that lack such a requirement. A “liquidated” debt is one where the amount is known or can be readily determined. (E.g., the amount owed at any moment under a loan may not be stated in the note but can be computed by reference to its terms.) title: At-Will Agencies, Vulnerable Insiders: How Trump v. Slaughter Imperils Whistleblower Adjudication - The National Law Review
content: The National Law Review uses cookies to track usage trends and patterns to better understand and improve our website. By using this website and/or clicking on any link on the website, you confirm your consent to the NLR’s placing and usage of cookies. On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court issued a watershed 6-3 ruling in Trump v. Slaughter, overruling the 91-year-old precedent of Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935). The case arose from President Donald Trump’s removal of Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Commissioner Rebecca Slaughter without alleging any statutory cause, such as “inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance in office.” The Court held that the FTC’s statutory for-cause removal protection violates the Constitution’s separation of powers, substantially expanding the President’s authority to remove the leaders of independent agencies at will. Writing for the majority, Chief Justice John Roberts anchored the decision in the Constitution’s Executive Vesting Clause (Article II, §1) and Take Care Clause (Article II, §3), holding that executive power is indivisible and vested in a single President. Invoking The Federalist Papers, the Court reasoned that democratic accountability demands a strict administrative hierarchy: because the President alone bears responsibility for the execution of federal law, agency officers are merely “assistants or deputies” who must remain subject to his plenary superintendence and at-will removal. While some scholars have framed Slaughter as a victory for the unitary executive theory and a restoration of original constitutional design, the decision carries significant consequences for administrative adjudication. For-cause removal protections provide institutional insulation by limiting the President’s ability to remove agency officials based solely on policy disagreements or political preference, allowing those officials to exercise their statutory responsibilities with greater independence from the acting administration. By eliminating statutory for-cause protections for FTC commissioners, the Court has also cast doubt on the independence of other agencies whose officials historically retained similar protections. For whistleblowers, the implications of this ruling are particularly consequential. Agencies such as the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), and, most importantly, the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB), occupy critical positions for investigating, adjudicating, and remedying whistleblower claims. In a dissent joined by Justices Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson, Justice Sonia Sotomayor warned that the majority’s sweeping rejection of precedent would fundamentally alter the balance of power, granting the President “a power unknown even to the English Crown against which the Founders revolted.” The dissent emphasizes that this unchecked executive authority directly overrides the will of Congress, which has long structured multimember commissions with bipartisan membership and staggered terms precisely to shield independent agencies from short-term partisan pressures. Justice Sotomayor also highlighted the majority’s failure to define the boundaries of its holding, cautioning that their rule “promises to unleash only chaos.” By leaving the status of quasi-judicial bodies such as the MSPB and NLRB unresolved while articulating a broad constitutional principle favoring executive control, the Court has undermined the structural independence of agencies central to whistleblower adjudication. One of the most consequential institutions implicated by Slaughter is the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB), the quasi-judicial agency responsible for adjudicating employment disputes within the federal civil service under the Whistleblower Protection Act (WPA) of 1989. For the civil service merit system to properly function, MSPB adjudicators must be able to rule against executive leadership without fearing employment retaliation themselves. Under Slaughter, however, an administration threatened by whistleblower disclosures could remove MSPB Board members without statutory cause and replace them with political loyalists. This dynamic would create a chilling effect across all executive agencies: civil servants will hesitate to report wrongdoing if their ultimate court of appeal is beholden to the very executive leadership they are exposing. The risks of an unfettered unitary executive were not unforeseen. In an amicus curiae brief submitted to the Court for Slaughter, the National Whistleblower Center (NWC) urged the Court to preserve Congress’s authority to establish statutory removal safeguards. Drawing on debates from the First Congress in 1789, the amici argue that the Framers of the Constitution reserved to Congress the power to define executive removal authority, with Supreme Court jurisprudence affirming as such. The NWC underscored that unchecked presidential removal power renders federal whistleblowers particularly vulnerable to retaliation. The experience of Dr. Tommie “Toni” G. Savage, a decorated Army whistleblower and NWC board member, serves as a stark illustration of this reality. After exposing widespread contract fraud within the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, final enforcement remedies were stalled for a decade until the MSPB finally ruled in her favor. In 2025, however, her case was placed on indefinite hold when the President removed the MSPB Chair without cause, dispossessing the Board of its quorum and incapacitating its ability to issue her long-awaited final order. The fallout of Slaughter extends beyond Washington’s civil service, even disrupting corporate and financial regulators such as the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC). Under the Dodd-Frank Act of 2010, Congress codified mandatory reward frameworks for whistleblowers to the SEC and CFTC. This law requires payment of 10%–30% of collected monetary sanctions to whistleblowers who voluntarily provide “original information” to these agencies, provided their information leads to successful enforcement actions exceeding $1 million. Congress also structured these key programs with quasi-judicial appeal mechanisms. If the Claims Review Staff issues a Preliminary Determination denying an award or reducing its percentage, the whistleblower is entitled to an administrative petition reviewed by the full Commission. Under Slaughter’s at-will removal regime, however, the structural neutrality of this process is subject to partisan influence. Existing law gives the SEC and CFTC discretion to determine the exact award percentage based on various balancing criteria such as the significance of the information or the degree of assistance. If commissioners serve at presidential will, the administration can exert pressure to systematically depress award amounts, deny claims arising from investigations into politically sensitive corporations, or even reinterpret regulations to serve partisan ends. An at-will Commission forfeits its political independence. Without for-cause insulation, agency executives are compelled to abide by the political agenda of a particular administration—or risk retaliation themselves. With administrative agencies susceptible to political interference, federal whistleblowers now face a pressing deficit. The Slaughter decision has created an urgent need for Congress to reconsider whether whistleblower protections should depend so heavily on the institutional independence of executive agencies. One legislative response is the Congressional Whistleblower Protection Act of 2025 (S. 1154), introduced by Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) in March of 2025. The bill puts forward expanded protections for federal employees, contractors, and other covered individuals who face retaliation for making protected disclosures. It also provides eligible whistleblowers with access to federal courts and the right to a jury trial. By shifting the adjudication of covered whistleblower claims from executive-branch bodies to Article III courts, S. 1154 would strengthen the structural neutrality of the enforcement process by placing factual disputes before independent judges and juries rather than agency-appointed adjudicators. Unlike administrative board members, federal district court judges hold life tenure and salary protections under Article III, shielding them from at-will presidential removal. The legislation thus provides federal whistleblowers a judicial forum insulated from partisan pressure, reducing the risk that civil servants like Dr. Savage will be left without meaningful recourse. The bill has remained stalled in the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs since its introduction. In the wake of Slaughter, however, legislation that places meritorious whistleblower claims before Article III courts deserves renewed consideration. The holding in Trump v. Slaughter emphasizes the tension between democratic accountability and bureaucratic independence. From the majority’s perspective, at-will removal vindicates Article II of the Constitution by ensuring that all discretionary executive power is accountable to an elected President, who in turn remains accountable to the voting public. Yet in pursuing a hierarchical model of administrative power, the Court overlooks a fundamental constitutional principle: that certain public integrity functions forfeit their legitimacy the moment they bend to partisan pressure. Whistleblower adjudication presents a particularly acute litmus test of administrative independence, as the claimant’s interest is often directly opposed to the interests of executive leadership. An agency cannot inspire public confidence merely by possessing the authority to rule against the government; it must also be functionally insulated from the officials whose conduct it is called upon to scrutinize. The repercussions of Slaughter do not lie in an abstract restructuring of administrative law, but in the deterrence of internal accountability. Until Congress acts to bridge this gap, every whistleblower who stands up to corruption and fraud will be left navigating a system where political loyalty threatens to eclipse the rule of law. title: Exclusive: Butler's new, tiny, chill mascot Blue V gives IndyStar one-on-one interview - IndyStar
content: INDIANAPOLIS — April Kirts isn't saying for sure that the tiny, red fawn, white-accented English bulldog lying next to her with beautiful rolls forming on his stout body and massive paws plopped on his miniature couch, was destined to be the next live mascot for Butler University. But how do you explain Blue V's aversion to the carpet in Kirts' house, which covers the entire living room? He's always searching for hardwood or a cool place to relax. "Right now, his favorite spot in the house is underneath my coffee table on the lower ledge," says Kirts, Blue V's handler. "It's the only hardwood we've got in our living room." It seems to be fate that Blue V is Butler's new mascot, taking over the hallowed court of Hinkle Fieldhouse as successor to Blue IV, who retired in February. For now, he is a 12-week-old, 13-pound mascot-in-training, gaining weight by the second. And, he is a bundle, not of energy but of pure, unadulterated, adorable chill. To be fair, Kirts says, Blue V can be much more energetic, but he had spent the morning at Bark Tutor, where he is getting intense training. "That can definitely wear him out," Kirts said. "He's pretty mellow, but he is pretty playful at heart. So, as much as he loves to sleep and just lay around, he also does love to play with other dogs and hang out with people. But overall, he likes to kind of just chill and hang out." Blue V is on track to graduate from his school in three weeks. After that, he and Kirts will work one-on-one with a trainer to hone their skills. For Kirts, a 2026 Butler grad, becoming Blue V's handler "was kind of like a pinch-me moment." Blue V yawns and stretches as Kirts tells her story. Blue V is just a baby, after all. But he's about to be thrown into the spotlight of the college basketball-loving world of mascot mania. On Friday afternoon, Blue V made his debut during a campus celebration, introduced to the world as Butler's new mascot. Friday night, he will make his appearance at the Butler-Pitt men’s basketball game at Hinkle. Two days before his big moment came, Blue V and Kirts gave IndyStar an exclusive interview. Blue V was one of six male bulldogs born Aug. 17 to parents Rory and Diva in Sorento, Ill. When Kirts and other members of Butler’s marketing team met the litter to pick the next Butler Blue, the choice became evident early on. "He was playful and easygoing, but what stood out was how comfortable he seemed with everyone," Kirts said. "He was curious, affectionate and full of personality. He also seemed to know exactly what to do when we brought out the camera. "We felt like he kind of chose us in a similar way that we chose him." Kirts graduated from Butler in May 2026 with a degree in journalism and a minor in strategic communication. She grew up with dogs and was drawn to Butler's live mascot program even before enrolling as a student. When the position in Butler's marketing department to be Blue V's handler opened, Kirts received a message from her Butler professor and mentor Bob Schultz. He asked Kirts if she liked dogs and if she was passionate about Butler. Kirts grew up with Newfoundlands. Her family has one Newfoundland now, along with a Shih Tzu. Blue V will go home with Kirts to Illinois to celebrate Thanksgiving and meet her family. "So he's a mascot, but he really acts as an all-campus ambassador," Kirts says. "He'll go to basketball games, meet prospective students, meet with a lot of alumni, people like that, and kind of just support the Butler community wherever he can." "Our main focus is basic commands and potty training," Kirts says. "He's still kind of figuring out how his body works and how his legs are growing." As Kirts explains Blue V's future, he stretches out and yawns. Right now, he's got sleeping to do. Butler's connection to the bulldog dates to 1919, when a bulldog named Shimmy wandered into the offices of The Butler Collegian. A cartoon of Shimmy appeared on the front page of the next issue, helping establish the bulldog as the university's mascot. While unofficial live mascots appeared throughout the decades, Butler established its official live mascot program in 2000. Since then, four Butler Blues and their handlers have transformed the program into one of the university's most recognizable traditions. title: Davis V. Goliath: a small town fight against big data - WLBT
content: TUCKER COUNTY, W.Va. — Data centers were on the ballot for the first time in a U.S. election, according to Ballotpedia, which counted 47 local ballot measures dealing with data centers in the midterms. Voters chose to curb data center development in their communities in 46 of them. Residents of one West Virginia community said they were not given that choice. The small mountain town in Tucker County is home to the Blackwater River and twin ski mountains. Tourism is the town’s lifeblood, and a proposed 10,000-acre natural gas-powered data center now threatens it. Jane Browning, owner of Ranger Jane, said tourism makes up most of her business. “Tourism is 80 percent of my business, and if there’s no tourism, there’s no business,” Browning said. If completed, the data center would be the largest in the world, measuring slightly smaller than Manhattan. West Virginia Gov. Patrick Morrisey believes the project will be a boon for the state. “We’re going to make sure that the water’s addressed, the environment’s addressed, that the power bills are lower, it’s going to get handled the right way,” Morrisey said. Residents described the situation differently. One said, “It came out of nowhere, there was no warning, there was no opportunity to say no.” Another said, “We were never given a choice, never given a voice.” A third said, “There’s something here that we don’t know.” North Carolina-based developer Ted McGavran of Fundamental Data said on a hot mic in July why West Virginia was chosen. “Up in West Virginia, we’re the guys that wrote the bill and got it through the Legislature. We can do pretty much whatever we want to do up there,” McGavran said. The bill’s sponsor is West Virginia Speaker of the House Roger Hanshaw. Hanshaw also serves as the lawyer for Fundamental Data, the company behind the project. Multiple requests for comment have not received a response. Morrisey maintains the state is acting in good faith and said, “Nothing’s been approved.” Public filings show the project’s air permits were approved Aug. 15. The issue has reached Washington. Sens. Martin Heinrich and Sheldon Whitehouse are introducing a data center permitting reform bill. “When a community is considering whether or not to grant a permit to a major data center, it needs to understand what that project will mean for its electricity supply. Cost, water resources, infrastructure and local economy. In order for them to make a good decision,” Sen. Heinrich said.

title: 2028 Ford Mustang Cobra with a Race Car-Derived V-8 Is Worth Waiting For - Car and Driver
content: The Cobra finally returns to the Mustang lineup and essentially resumes the track-focused role last held by the Shelby GT350. Ford only just launched the Mustang Dark Horse SC earlier this year, but the Blue Oval brand isn’t letting up when it comes to high-performance versions of its iconic pony car. While the S650-generation Mustang introduced the new Dark Horse branding—at the expense of the legendary Shelby nameplate—and saw the arrival of the new $300,000-plus GTD, Ford’s upcoming Mustang variant revives a famous name from the past: Cobra. The new Mustang Cobra is expected to slot between the Dark Horse and Dark Horse SC as an indirect successor to the last Shelby GT350, providing track-ready performance and high-fidelity driver engagement. The Shelby GT350, offered from 2015–2020, is considered one of the best Mustangs ever, thanks to its naturally aspirated flat-plane-crank 5.2-liter V-8 known as Voodoo. The last Cobra is also coveted by Mustang fans, so the new track-focused model has big shoes to fill. And with a new engine most likely under the Cobra’s hood, there’s potential for another legendary Mustang to be born. See all results for new 2028 Ford Mustang for sale near 50317 The Cobra will continue to utilize the S650 platform, itself an evolution of the S550 chassis that underpinned the Mustang from 2015–2023. The Cobra will adapt the Mustang into a dedicated track car, and we think it will also spawn a more hardcore Cobra R with even more extreme aerodynamics, stronger brakes, and greater weight savings, potentially even removing the backseat. We expect the Cobra’s bodywork to be based on the Dark Horse SC, but with small tweaks and possibly a rear wing that harkens back to the 2000 Cobra R. Mustang fans are obviously clamoring for the return of the Voodoo, but we don’t think that’s what Ford has in store. Fret not, however, because the automaker is cooking up something special for the new Cobra. Instead of the 5.2-liter Voodoo, the new Cobra will pack a naturally aspirated 5.4-liter engine derived from the Mustang GT3 race car that has triumphed at the 24 Hours of Daytona and secured a podium at Le Mans. The Coyote-based GT3 engine features a cross-plane crank, but the teaser video released by Ford emitted a high-revving scream, so there’s a chance that the Cobra’s engine will switch to a flat-plane-crank setup. Still, if you’ve recently been to an IMSA race, you’ll know the GT3 car produces a thunderous soundtrack, so enthusiasts are in for an auditory treat regardless. Although Ford hasn’t confirmed that the Cobra will adapt the GT3 race car’s engine, in the first teaser it said the car would pack a “heart born from racing.” We don’t expect the Cobra to come close to the Dark Horse SC or GTD in terms of power, but we wouldn’t be shocked if the 5.4-liter V-8 exceeds the 550 horsepower that the GT3 car is restricted to by racing regulations. We think Ford will likely employ the Tremec TR-3160 transmission already used in the Dark Horse. At the moment, the Mustang has the V-8 muscle car world all to itself. Dodge is expected to stuff a supercharged V-8 back into the Charger for the 2028 model year, while Chevy is gearing up to bring back the Camaro around 2028. The only other V-8-powered car under $100,000 is the Corvette, which has a completely different form factor with its mid-engine layout, but it will likely still be cross-shopped against the Cobra. Pricing is probably the biggest risk. Ford needs to make sure it doesn’t alienate its customers by making it too expensive, given that the Dark Horse SC already has a hefty $105,585 asking price (about $20K more than the GT500 that it replaced). The new 5.4-liter V-8 will also have to make a strong impression as a successor to the much-loved Voodoo. The Mustang Cobra will likely be revealed in early 2027 and go on sale before the end of the year. We expect pricing to start somewhere in the $80,000 range, but it could easily climb to $100,000 for a Cobra R model.
